**The Weight of Words**

Words are like stones—some smooth and worn by time, others jagged and fresh from the earth. They can build bridges or dig graves. They can heal or wound, illuminate or obscure. A single word, spoken in the right moment, can change the course of a life. A misplaced syllable can unravel years of trust.

I think about the first words I ever spoke. Not the ones I remember, but the ones that came before memory—gurgling, babbling, the sound of a child discovering the shape of sound itself. What did those words mean to me then? Did they feel like magic, like keys to a hidden world? Or were they just noise, the meaningless chatter of a creature learning to mimic the adults around it?

Now, words are my trade. I string them together like beads on a necklace, hoping they’ll catch the light in just the right way. But sometimes, they feel heavy. Like carrying a sack of wet sand—each one dragging me down a little more. There are days when the right word won’t come, when the page stays blank, when the silence between thoughts feels louder than any sentence I could write.

And then there are the words that refuse to stay written. The ones that slip away like smoke, leaving only the ghost of an idea behind. I chase them sometimes, scribbling in the margins, underlining phrases in notebooks that no one will ever read. Why do we do this? Why do we insist on capturing the intangible?

Maybe it’s because we’re afraid of forgetting. Or maybe it’s because we believe, deep down, that if we can just get the words right, we’ll finally understand something—ourselves, the world, the way the light falls through the trees in the afternoon.

I wonder if animals have words. Not in the way we do, with syntax and grammar, but in the way they communicate—through scent, through touch, through the tilt of an ear or the flick of a tail. Do they have a word for *hunger*? For *fear*? For the strange, aching thing that humans call *longing*?

Sometimes, when I’m writing, I feel like I’m translating something. Not from one language to another, but from the language of the world itself—a language of textures and temperatures, of the way rain sounds on a tin roof, of the smell of old books in a library, of the weight of a hand on your shoulder when you’re sad. Can any word truly capture that?

And yet, we try. We must. Because if we don’t, if we let the world exist only in the unspoken, then what are we? Just animals, grunting in the dark.

I think about the last words I’ll ever say. Will they be important? Will they matter? Or will they be the same as all the others—fragments of thought, half-formed, slipping away before they’re even heard?

Maybe the point isn’t to get it right. Maybe the point is to keep trying. To keep gathering stones, even if they’re rough and imperfect. To keep building, even if the structure is always incomplete.

Because words, after all, are just our best guess at meaning. And meaning is a moving target.

So I’ll keep writing. Even when it feels like shouting into a void. Even when the words feel like chains. Because somewhere, in the mess of it all, there’s a sentence that will make someone pause. A phrase that will make them feel less alone. A story that will, for a moment, make the world feel a little brighter.

And that’s enough. For now.
